# About

Source: https://designerdan.github.io/about

## 12 years in. More whiteboard than mockup. Why before how.

**The work, by the numbers**

- **$860M** — Zix acquisition by OpenText
- **+21%** — Zix ARR increase post-launch
- **~40k** — Net new users at Zix
- **$1M+** — Pixly AI pipeline
- **90%+** — Pixly tag precision in testing
- **80** — Open Door Legal NPS

### Testimonial

> “Your perspective is intriguing and I enjoy the playfulness with which you seem to approach both life and work. When you ask questions and dig at the ‘why’ of what we are doing, you move us in a better direction.”

— President Improving Enterprises

### Who I am

Build-forward. Upstream of the interface.

I’m a build-forward person — focused on where you are, where you want to go, and the most direct path between the two. I don’t default to complexity when simplicity will do, and I don’t decorate problems. I try to understand them.

My best work happens upstream of the interface: data models, requirements, taxonomy decisions — the choices that determine whether the UI has a fighting chance before anyone opens Figma. A beautiful screen on top of a broken system is just an expensive distraction.

I care about craft in the functional sense — that the grid works, the interaction holds up at edge cases, and the thing actually ships. And I’m suspicious of buzzwords: if you can’t explain why a decision was made, it wasn’t a decision. It was just a thing that happened.

### What I value

#### Consideration

> Like someone charged with an ecosystem, I consider the parts for the whole.

Holistic design strategy — data, research, systems thinking, and craft working as one product decision, not separate deliverables.

#### Style

> I’ll get you to stand out where standing out matters.

Differentiation as an empathetic advantage — doing what’s different, filling the hole in the whole, for the people who need you.

#### Craft

> I elevate products beyond a means and into an experience.

Every element — color, typography, layout, interaction — considered so the product connects with people on a deeper level.

### My approach

Three products where the thinking shows up.

- **Enterprise Email Security** — 4 softwares. 1 design system. $860M exit.
- **Construction AI** — 3 weeks. 1 AI POC. Kiewit.
- **Legal Nonprofit SaaS** — Ethics review. Salesforce. 80 NPS.

### How I work

#### Work upstream of the interface.

Open Door Legal’s grant data model couldn’t relate one client to multiple grants. I defined a Beneficiary junction object as a requirement — the interface was the last thing designed, not the first.

#### Scale judgment, not control.

At a 70:1 engineer-to-designer ratio, owning every decision is a trap. I invested in a governed design system and engineering relationships so the right call got made without me in the room.

#### Treat constraints as the brief.

A California ethics attorney had to approve ODL’s referral flows; Pixly’s AI needed an 80% confidence threshold to earn trust. The limits told me exactly what the design had to do.

#### Sequence beats scope.

On Pixly I rejected AI branding and scoped provenance out of the POC — answering “does this work at all?” first. A validated proof of concept shipped in three weeks.

### What I’m looking for

> Seeking high-trust, high-performant builder environments with direct outcomes.

Based in San Francisco. Available for the right role, remote or in-person.

### Good-natured people with a sense of humor welcome.

If you value style, craft, and consideration from the people you work with — we’ll probably get along fine.

# Zix — Unifying apps across a merger

Source: https://designerdan.github.io/zix

## Unifying apps across a merger

**Key metrics**

- **$860M** — OpenText acquisition, Nov 2021
- **21%** — ARR increase post-launch
- **~40k** — net new users
- **4** — softwares merged

**Project details**

- **Project:** Design system and UX unification across 4 enterprise applications.
- **Contributions:** Design System, UX Ops, Interaction Design
- **Team:** UX Director, Engineering, Product Management
- **Client:** Zix
- **Timeline:** 12 months

### The business problem

Zix was operating separate softwares, each of them using a different design language, interaction patterns, and information architecture.

Enterprise buyers saw four separate products and had to judge the risk. Would the tools work together? Would staff need separate training? Could Zix support a larger, more complex account? A fragmented experience made the company look less mature at the moment trust mattered most.

### Product showcase

The goal: create a unified product experience across the suite without pausing roadmap work or forcing a costly rebuild.

- Research
- Audit
- Patterns
- System

### What was at stake

Zix was a moving enterprise product organization.

Four products were shipping in parallel, teams had different priorities, and I did not control every roadmap or product decision.

My job was not to redesign everything or approve every screen. It was to create a shared system that helped independent teams make more consistent, customer-centered decisions while the business kept moving.

### Decisions that mattered

#### Build influence into the system

I could not review every screen or control every product decision. Trying to do so would have made design a bottleneck and slowed teams already working against separate priorities. Instead, I created a shared decision framework. The design system included reusable components, documented interaction rules, clear states, and a single source of truth connected to engineering handoffs.

The tradeoff was intentional. I gave up control over some local product choices so teams could move faster with a reliable default for common customer workflows. This was not a visual style guide. It was a way to distribute product judgment across a large organization.

#### Unify the highest-value workflows first

A complete product redesign was not realistic. The portfolio needed visible progress while each team continued its roadmap work. I used a Top Tasks analysis and a cross-product pattern audit to identify the workflows customers encountered most often. The audit showed that users completed the same core tasks in different ways depending on the product they were using.

We prioritized the patterns with the broadest reach: tables, forms, dashboards, search, filters, bulk actions, error states, and administrative workflows. The tradeoff was that lower-priority inconsistencies remained in place for a time. In return, the program improved the areas customers used most often and gave teams concrete work they could ship in stages.

#### Improve familiar patterns instead of replacing them

Tables were the dominant interaction pattern across the portfolio. They supported core admin work such as reviewing data, sorting, filtering, managing accounts, and taking action on large sets of records. The problem was not that customers needed a new pattern. The problem was that every team had implemented the same pattern differently.

I chose to standardize and improve tables rather than replace them. The shared pattern defined column behavior, sort and filter rules, bulk actions, readable spacing, accessible target sizes, empty states, success messages, error handling, and undo actions. This reduced unnecessary learning for existing users while creating a more predictable experience across products.

### Banner

A fragmented product does not get acquired for $860M. A coherent one does.

### How I led the work

I began by making the problem visible.

I conducted an audit covering design patterns across 21 applications and showed where similar tasks had drifted into different workflows. I then turned those findings into practical guidance that teams could use. The system was built in Abstract and Sketch, with a single source of truth linked to engineering handoffs. Developers could access current components and interaction rules without relying on stale exports or repeated clarification.

The work also depended on relationships. I worked with engineering teams to understand implementation limits, clarify the intent behind patterns, and help teams apply the system to real product work. My role was to establish shared standards, make the right choice easier, and help teams understand when a workflow required a deliberate exception.

### What this demonstrates

This engagement shaped how I lead design in complex organizations.

When product teams are moving in parallel, central control does not scale. The work is to identify the decisions that should be shared, turn them into usable systems, and help teams apply them without waiting for permission. That is how enterprise design becomes durable: not through one designer owning every screen, but through many teams making better decisions with a common foundation.

**Image captions**

- Four products, four admin experiences — before anything could be unified.
- 21 apps meant 21 ways to do the same admin task.
- High-traffic admin flows after the shared table and form patterns landed.
- Partner admins manage thousands of accounts — filters and bulk actions had to scale.
- Quarantine — search 10,000 released messages, act on a page at a time.
- Allowed-list requests — approve the domain, deny the IP, save the rest for later.
- Domain protection — errors surfaced inline instead of after a failed save.
- Partners run O365 audits from one dashboard — schedule, track, and hand off reports.

### Impact

> “At first [this software] was annoying to use, but in recent years they've made it much easier to deal with.”

— Customer review Zix product user

In November 2021, OpenText acquired Zix for $860 million. In the year following the design system launch, Zix's ARR increased 21% per SEC filings, with approximately 40,000 net new users.

### Next project

3 weeks. 1 AI POC. Kiewit.

# Pixly — AI vision for construction photos

Source: https://designerdan.github.io/pixly

## AI vision for construction photos

**Key metrics**

- **$1M+** — Pipeline with Kiewit, Granite, Kahua
- **50%** — Of ENR 400 via SmartPM integration
- **3,056** — Users · 29 customers at POC delivery
- **90%+** — Tag precision validated in testing

**Project details**

- **Project:** AI-powered auto-tagging and content-indexed search for construction photo documentation.
- **Contributions:** UX Research, Interaction Design, Tag Taxonomy
- **Partners:** SnapSoft (AI/ML), Carnera (UI), Pixly
- **Client:** Pixly.ai
- **Timeline:** 3 weeks

### The business problem

Pixly helps construction teams capture jobsite photos. Capture worked. Finding the photo later, not so much.

Field teams take hundreds of photos per project. Photos document safety issues, progress, materials, equipment, and site conditions. Pixly needed to test whether AI-powered tagging and content-based search could make its existing photo library easier to use.

### Product showcase

The goal: test whether automatic image tagging and content-based search could help construction teams find project photos faster.

- Capture
- Albums
- Tags
- Search

### What was at stake

Pixly was becoming a place where teams stored photos but could not retrieve knowledge.

A product like that would be easy to replace and weaken Pixly's position in a market where documentation, proof, and reporting matter.

There was also a product-risk question. AI features can sound compelling in sales conversations but fail when users see wrong or irrelevant results. The work needed to protect trust while proving that automated tagging could improve retrieval in real jobsite conditions.

The three-week timeline raised the delivery risk. Every decision had to serve the central question. Time spent on advanced features would reduce time available to validate whether the core workflow worked.

### Decisions that mattered

#### Prove one useful customer outcome first

The team could have treated AI tagging as a broad platform effort. That would mean designing provenance, advanced library management, collaborative tagging, rich faceted navigation, and many possible AI features before learning whether users trusted the basics.

I recommended a narrower first bet: tag photos automatically at capture, map those tags to terms construction teams actually use, and make the results useful in search.

The tradeoff was deliberate. We deferred features that would matter in a mature tagging product so we could answer the first business question quickly: would people use AI-generated tags to find their work?

#### Design for trust, not just tag accuracy

Computer vision can produce a label even when it is uncertain. Showing every predicted tag would create noisy search results and weaken trust. Hiding too much would reduce the value of the system.

I worked with the team to set an 80% confidence threshold. Tags above that threshold appeared in search results. Tags below it stayed in the index but did not appear until a user confirmed or rejected them.

The tradeoff was recall versus trust. We chose to show fewer results when the model was unsure because one clearly wrong result can damage confidence more than one missing result. This also created a feedback loop. User confirmation could improve the system without making uncertain AI behavior visible as a product failure.

#### Translate AI labels into field language

The AI could identify objects, but its labels did not always match the words people used on construction sites. A generic label such as “excavating equipment” was technically correct, but a superintendent was more likely to search for “excavator” or “backhoe.”

I owned the vocabulary layer between model output and user behavior. I combined generic image labels with construction-specific labels and created a synonym map that matched the language field users used to describe materials, equipment, and site conditions.

The tradeoff was more work up front. Without it, Pixly could claim technical accuracy while still failing the user's real task: finding photos with the words that came naturally to them.

### Banner

Search that speaks their language, not a bolt-on feature.

### How I led the work

I began with contextual inquiry across three construction firms.

The research showed two distinct needs. Field users needed to find a specific photo quickly, often from memory. Project managers needed to browse a category of photos across a project, such as concrete work, equipment, or a site condition.

It also showed that chronology was the wrong organizing model. People did not think, “Show me photos from Tuesday.” They thought, “Show me the concrete pour on the east wing,” or “Find all photos of the excavator.”

I used those findings to align the partners around shared product decisions. The AI team had a clear definition of useful labels. The UI team had a clear search model and interaction direction. Pixly had a focused POC that connected technical capability to customer value.

### Technical integration

The vocabulary problem I had to own.

AWS Rekognition produces generic object labels. SageMaker custom models produce domain labels—rebar types, concrete conditions, equipment models. The taxonomy had to merge both into one vocabulary that matched how field users actually spoke.

SnapSoft's initial label set didn't map to field vocabulary. “Excavating equipment” isn't what Marcus says; “excavator” and “backhoe” are. Building the synonym map required sitting between ML output and user research—forcing an alignment neither party was initially scoping for.

### What I would change

The AI and UX work began with too much asynchronous back-and-forth on taxonomy decisions.

Bringing the ML and UX teams together during the first sprint would have reduced a lost week and produced faster alignment.

That experience reinforced a principle I use in AI product work: model quality and product meaning cannot be designed in isolation. The technology may identify an object, but the product still has to decide what it means, when to show it, and whether users can trust it.

### What this demonstrates

I choose small, credible bets that prove concepts.

I don't go all in until the concept is proven. When I do I make sure to lead across research, interaction design, and partner alignment. I did not own the ML pipeline or the visual UI team for this engagement but I did own the decisions that connected those moving parts to a clear customer outcome.

**Image captions**

- Tagging runs in the photo viewer — not a separate admin screen.
- Same feed serves field capture and desktop retrieval workflows.
- System photo picker for batch upload from the device camera roll.
- Tag names and counts after merging ML labels with field vocabulary.
- Batch upload on desktop; tagging status shown per thumbnail.
- Mobile album grid shows tag counts while batch tagging runs.
- Sidebar tag list matches numbered pins on the photo.
- Tags appear as numbered pins on the photo.
- Album grid after batch tagging finishes.
- Tag search and placement use the same Tag Library sheet.
- Search bar above feed accepts text and image input.
- Issue tag count shown separately from other tag types.
- General tag grid with edit and delete actions per row.
- Issue filter applied in photo viewer sidebar.

### Impact

> “Pixly saves us time and resources and has streamlined our photo documentation process. It's an absolute game-changer!”

— Tim Van Hook, Director of Learning & Development, Kitchen Saver

Tag accuracy validated above 90% precision during the AWS-funded POC. The path to full deployment is open—with $1M+ pipeline unlocked with Kiewit, Granite, and Kahua.

# Open Door Legal — Infrastructure for Legal Tech

Source: https://designerdan.github.io/odl

## Infrastructure for Legal Tech

**Key metrics**

- **80** — NPS (120-day target)
- **-16%** — Referral redundancies
- **90%** — Grant admin reduction target
- **2** — Phases · client returned without RFP

**Project details**

- **Project:** Two-sided referral marketplace and grant management system in Salesforce.
- **Contributions:** UX Design, Stakeholder Alignment
- **Team:** Product Manager, Engineer, Me
- **Client:** Open Door Legal
- **Timeline:** 6 months

### The business problem

Open Door Legal is a San Francisco nonprofit that helps people access legal support across housing, immigration, and family law.

Its staff handle a high volume of client intakes and referrals. When a client needed help outside ODL's direct services, staff had to find a partner organization, contact them through separate channels, track the referral manually, and follow up outside the system. This manual process was time-consuming, error-prone, and made it difficult to monitor the referral process or identify gaps in service.

### Product showcase

The goal: build a two-sided referral marketplace in Salesforce, then create a grant-management foundation that reduced reporting overhead without placing compliance work on front-line staff.

- Compliance
- Onboarding
- Management
- Workflows

### What was at stake

A weak referral system introduced risk under California professional-conduct rules.

A weak grant-management system could create inaccurate funder reports, staff burnout, and risk to grant renewal. For a nonprofit, reporting quality is directly connected to the ability to continue providing services.

The design challenge was to improve operational speed without asking case managers to become compliance experts. The system had to guide them through the right steps while preserving the focus on the client.

### Decisions that mattered

#### Treat consent and confidentiality as product states

The referral process involved sharing client information with outside legal organizations. That is not a standard handoff. Attorneys have duties around confidentiality, informed consent, and prospective clients.

The easy approach would have been to treat consent as a checkbox and rely on staff training to prevent mistakes. That would leave too much room for an incorrect action during a busy workflow.

I recommended making consent, data visibility, conflict status, and partner eligibility explicit states in the product. Staff could see what was allowed, what information would be shared, and what had to happen before a referral could move forward. The tradeoff was a more structured workflow. In return, the system reduced reliance on memory and helped staff make the safe choice at the moment it mattered.

#### Make referrals self-contained

Salesforce often spreads work across related lists, tabs, and separate records. That can work for low-risk CRM tasks, but it creates friction when staff need to understand, act on, and close a referral quickly.

I designed the referral as a self-contained object. Everything needed to process the referral, communicate with a partner, track the client's status, and close the loop appeared in one workflow. The tradeoff was moving away from default Salesforce navigation patterns. The benefit was lower context switching and a clearer view of what remained to be done.

A closed referral also needed an intentional end state. Staff needed to know that the work was complete so they could return to their queue without wondering whether an action had been missed.

#### Build grant reporting into the data model

The grant-management problem could not be solved with cleaner screens alone. ODL needed to connect one client to multiple grants, activities, intakes, cases, outcomes, and time forecasts. Without those relationships, staff would keep reconciling reports by hand. That created administrative cost, reporting errors, and funding risk.

I helped define the Beneficiary junction object as the architectural link between the client, grant activities, and related service records. This made per-funder reporting possible without manual reconstruction of the client's service history.

The tradeoff was investing in upstream data-model work before designing the final interface. The benefit was a system that could produce reliable reporting and reduce the burden on staff.

### Banner

Phase 1 results: NPS hit the 120-day target of 80. They came back for Phase 2 without a competitive process.

### How I led the work

I started by mapping how staff actually worked and where the system failed the process.

The existing workflows relied on an external databases, manual contact through several channels, and hand-entered status tracking.

I translated that reality into a two-sided workflow for referrers, receiving partners, and the system itself. I brought the client into regular reviews, tested the flows, and worked through the exceptions that made the difference between a polished concept and an operational product.

For grant management, I shifted upstream. The first question was not what the screen should look like. It was what objects needed to exist, how they needed to relate, and which data had to be captured during intake and case closure.

That work made it possible to surface grant-relevant fields at the right moment. Staff did not need to remember reporting rules separately from serving clients.

### What this engagement required that most don't

#### Ethics as a design constraint.

The consequences of a wrong interaction state aren't a bad user experience—they're a professional conduct violation. That forced precision in consent flows, data visibility, and state communication I'd carry into any high-stakes domain work.

#### Guiding line staff without burdening them.

Case managers shouldn't need to think about grant compliance. Intake finalization and case close flows surface grant-relevant fields at the exact moment they're needed—and prevent progression unless required data is entered.

#### Working upstream of the UI.

The grant data model work required operating at the boundary of UX and systems design—defining what objects needed to exist and how they needed to relate before any screens could be meaningful.

### What this demonstrates

How I turn legal, operational, and data constraints into safer products that work in the real world.

This project required more than workflow design. It required judgment about what should be automated, what information should remain limited, and how legal and funding constraints could become useful product behavior. I did not treat ethics, compliance, or data structure as constraints added after the design. I used them to define the product from the start.

That is how I approach high-stakes systems: make the safe path clear, make the real workflow visible, and build the underlying structure before asking the interface to solve a problem it cannot solve on its own.

### Results

> “You're the best designer we've ever had.”

— Executive Director Open Door Legal

NPS hit the 120-day target of 80 following the referral feature launch. Redundancies in referral handling were down 16% at measurement. Phase 2 grant management is in QA ahead of deployment—the 90% administration reduction is the production hypothesis.
